doc.title: Al Vollmer interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, June 8, 2017

chapter: Discovering jazz in Sweden and at Hamilton
title: Jelly Roll Morton at Hamilton and jazz in wartime Sweden
summary: Vollmer hears a Jelly Roll Morton record from an upperclassman's room, and explains he grew up in Sweden, where he discovered swing through Glenn Miller and Joe Loss records.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Well actually it was a Jelly Roll Morton record that was coming out of Carnegie Hall. So I knew it had to be upperclassmen, it wasn’t my class. We were all in South Dorm. And so I went in and I found where it was coming from and met some upperclassmen because of that, one of them particularly, Bill Robbins as I remember.
Why did you already know this music before you got to Hamilton?

Okay. I grew up from the age of 10 outside of Stockholm, Sweden. And I came to the United States when I was 17. So I lived in Sweden between the age of 10 and 17. And when we were 15 or 16, a number of us started getting interested in — well it was during the war, so not too much was coming into Sweden, but we did see the movie “Sun Valley Serenade,” which had Glenn Miller, “Chattanooga Choo Choo” and all of that, and “In the Mood.” And so we were excited by that, and we could get the Joe Loss recording of “In the Mood,” which was a British recording which was a total cover of the Glenn Miller recording.

Yes, Joe Loss was a bandleader in England who recorded for HMV. And he had a band that was quite famous and we could get — somehow or other that recording was available. Eventually I even got perhaps the most original recording which was the Edgar Hayes recording because that had Joe Garland in it, and Joe Garland wrote the tune.
